subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical laboratory solution contains 0.15 mol/L Na+ and 0.02 mol/L Ca2+, with chloride as the only anion present. What must the chloride concentration be, and what principle sets it?

options.text: 0.19 mol/L, because the total negative charge must balance the total positive charge
0.17 mol/L, because the total moles of anion must match the total moles of cation one for one
0.13 mol/L, because the divalent calcium offsets part of the sodium contribution
0.34 mol/L, because each dissolved cation requires two chloride ions to be neutralized

explanation:
Electroneutrality requires equal totals of positive and negative charge: 0.15 from Na+ plus 0.02 x 2 = 0.04 from Ca2+ gives 0.19 mol/L of positive charge. Chloride is monovalent, so 0.19 mol/L of Cl- is needed to balance it. Simply adding cation moles gives 0.17 and ignores calcium's 2+ valence, which is exactly the error that charge-based equivalents are designed to prevent. Bulk solutions cannot carry any appreciable net charge.

ELI-10: Balance charges, not particles. Sodium contributes 0.15 mol/L of ions each carrying one positive charge, so 0.15 units of positive charge. Calcium contributes only 0.02 mol/L of ions, but each carries two positive charges, so 0.02 x 2 = 0.04 units. The positive total is 0.19. Chloride carries one negative charge apiece, so its concentration must also be 0.19 mol/L. Counting calcium as 0.02 would leave the solution with net positive charge, which no real bulk solution can sustain.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
